headline: The National Popular Vote and the End of the Electoral College as We Know It

paragraphs.text: Beneath the surface of the upheaval in American politics that took place on Nov. 3, there were tremors of what could ultimately be an even bigger political earthquake: the end of the Electoral College as we know it.

Voters in Michigan, Wisconsin, Pennsylvania, Arizona and Nevada elected Democratic governors and secured Democratic majorities in their legislatures. The trifectas — control of the governor’s office and both state legislative chambers — open the door to the imminent adoption of the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact.

The compact is an agreement among states to award their presidential electoral votes to the nationwide popular vote winner. It goes into effect only when states having at least 270 electoral votes join it. The effort began more than two decades ago and has been quietly pushing toward a major transformation of American politics and government.

If these five states, which together have 61 electoral votes, sign the compact, then as early as November 2028, we could experience something no one has ever seen: a presidential election in which all Americans’ votes count equally and the candidate who gets the most votes wins.

Just imagine: The nation’s leader being elected by a majority (or at least a plurality) of the nation’s voters. Candidates campaigning all across the country because all votes matter. No more red states or blue states, just Americans everywhere casting ballots that actually count. It sounds almost magical, doesn’t it?

Every other election in the country already runs this way, and a majority of Americans have for decades said they want the presidential election to run this way, too. We say this because it is the natural expectation of citizens living in a modern representative democracy.

The arc of the American story has been, in slow and sometimes halting fashion, the vindication of democratic principles through the expansion of voting rights and of popular participation in government. Most of the original barriers to that participation have fallen — from the denial of voting rights to women, Black people and young adults to the selection of senators by state legislatures. The Electoral College, as it operates today, is the last major barrier.

So why not just amend it out of the Constitution, the way those other barriers were toppled? At the moment, that is a nonstarter. There have been more than 700 proposed amendments to change or abolish the Electoral College over the nation’s history, far more than for any other single provision of the Constitution. Yet it survives, a testament to the power of partisan politics, which has derailed so many reform efforts.

Critics of the compact argue that an amendment is the only acceptable way to enact such a sweeping change to American government. “The valid methods for amending the Constitution are specified” in the document itself, the Cato Institute argued, “and an agreement among a minority of states is not one of them.” They see the compact as an end run around the Constitution and fear, among other things, that a popular vote would result in big cities dominating every election. That latter claim, like so many about the Electoral College and the popular vote, is not true. (If “big cities,” which is usually code for “liberal areas,” actually dominate, how did Donald Trump win the popular vote in 2024?)

States that join the compact agree to use the constitutional power they possess to change how they award their electoral votes. Rather than award them all to the candidate who wins the most votes in the state, as 48 of 50 states currently do, states in the compact (there are 18 so far, plus Washington, D.C.) legally bind themselves to award their electoral votes to the popular vote winner of the entire country.

While there is no official national popular vote total, it’s not hard to come up with one. All 50 states and D.C. are already required by federal law to certify the electors they are appointing no later than six days before the Electoral College meets and those electors cast their ballots, which happens in mid-December. That certification must include final popular vote totals. From there, it’s just adding up the state totals — arithmetic a grade-school pupil could do.
In short, the vote-counting process would run exactly the same as it does today; the difference would be in how the states award their electoral votes.

Once states having a majority of electoral votes — 270 — join the compact, it turns the Electoral College into the vehicle for an election in which, by definition, the popular vote winner prevails every time. It doesn’t matter what other states do with their electors, because candidates will know that to win a majority of electoral votes, they have to win the most popular votes in the country, and they will campaign that way. It is an ingenious design and one that does not touch the Constitution.

The inventor of the compact, John Koza, is one of the more dogged and precise men I’ve ever met. He is an 83-year-old computer scientist who lives in Silicon Valley. After the 2000 election, when George W. Bush won the presidency despite trailing his opponent, Al Gore, by half a million popular votes, Mr. Koza started the compact, which he called National Popular Vote.

He has since devoted most of his waking hours to changing how Americans elect their president. We first met in 2019, when I was writing a book about the Electoral College and the compact, and we have corresponded regularly since. A few days after the election, I called to ask him whether he had been prepared for what happened on election night.

“Well, yeah,” he said matter-of-factly. “We’ve talked to almost every legislator in the five states; we targeted them 18 months ago.” He then went down the list and told me exactly where each state stood in terms of its likelihood of passing the compact.

I have learned over the years not to underestimate Mr. Koza’s attention to detail. He is the lead author of a book (revised at least four times and now 1,200 pages) that lays out the Electoral College’s history and the compact’s function and that rebuts seemingly every defense of the Electoral College and every challenge to a national popular vote that you could imagine.

At the same time, I have been a skeptic about how likely the compact is to pass: After an initial burst of states joining it, by the mid-2010s, it seemed to be languishing. Except for Hawaii, whose Republican governor’s veto had been overridden, all member states were led by Democratic governors when they joined, and there seemed to be little prospect of Republican buy-in.

That was, by itself, a big stumbling block. If the compact looked like a Democratic plot to win all presidential elections (Democrats won the popular vote in seven of the eight elections before 2024), it would be hard to convince Americans that this was being done for politically neutral reasons.

But the politics turn out to be not so simple. There was a time, before Mr. Trump, when some Republican lawmakers were very interested in the compact. Republican-led legislative chambers in Arizona, Oklahoma and New York all passed it, and it enjoyed significant Republican support in Georgia, Utah and Michigan. Yet after Mr. Trump won the White House in 2016 while losing the popular vote, that interest evaporated.

Even some Democratic leaders got cold feet. In May 2019, after the Nevada Legislature voted to join the compact, the state’s Democratic governor, Steve Sisolak, vetoed it. Since then, a few more states have joined, bringing the total number of electoral votes held by states in the compact to 222 — 48 short of 270. But it was hard to identify enough states left on the map to clear the bar.

Now, with those five states newly controlled by Democrats, it’s not hard at all. “I’m a little stunned,” Chris Pearson, an executive director at National Popular Vote, told me after Election Day. “But it felt well within the realm of possibility for months now.”

In Michigan, the compact had been co-sponsored by the incoming State House speaker and Senate majority leader; in Arizona, it previously passed one legislative chamber with bipartisan support. All five states have now elected an incoming governor or legislative leaders who have supported the compact. As soon as the next legislative session begins in 2027, those states could join the compact and push it past 270 electoral votes.

It’s difficult to overstate what a big deal this would be. The election of the president by popular vote would vindicate the fundamental democratic principles of political equality and majority rule in the most important election of all. It would also reverberate across the American political system, said Maria Collett, Pennsylvania’s incoming State Senate majority leader, who introduced popular vote compact legislation this year and plans to do so again next year.

Right now, Ms. Collett asked, “if you’re a Democratic voter in a deep-red state, what difference does it make” if you vote? The same goes for Republican voters in deep-blue states. “When people sit out elections, it hurts down-ballot candidates, people are less engaged, and we have fewer opportunities to make sure people feel heard,” she said. That, in turn, has a corrosive effect on the people’s sense of their power to choose their leaders. In contrast, “when we say every single vote counts, I think that adds to people feeling empowered,” Ms. Collett explained.
But it’s not only the good things a popular vote would promote; it’s also the bad things it would prevent.

Consider the Stop the Steal movement in 2020 and 2021, which culminated in the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol. An effort to stop Congress’s certification of the vote that day was, in Mr. Trump’s and his supporters’ minds, justified by razor-thin vote margins in key battleground states, which they baselessly attributed to fraud and other irregularities. In contrast, the average margin in the national popular vote over the past half century has been almost seven million ballots — far too big to credibly dispute. “The country is clear,” Mr. Pearson told me. “Right now the system does not honor that and leaves us quite vulnerable.”

Narrow state vote margins are dangerous in other ways too: they incentivize lawmakers to pass countless laws making it harder for certain people to vote, and they make it easier for any people (or foreign powers) who really intend to meddle in an election to identify specific states, counties or even precincts where they can get the most bang for their buck.
What happens if the compact reaches 270 electoral votes? Nothing this significant in American politics happens without a fight. So let’s consider some obstacles.

One is political. Should such a profound shift in American politics take place without a constitutional amendment? As I mentioned, critics of the compact have long charged that it is an end run around the Constitution, a sneaky way for about half of the states to achieve something that has an impact on the entire country.

But the compact’s ingenuity lies precisely in its reliance on the Constitution, of which Article II gives the states total control over how they award their electoral votes. The Supreme Court has reaffirmed that multiple times, most recently in 2020, when it ruled unanimously in Chiafalo v. Washington that Article II conveys to states “the broadest power of determination” over electors.

Today most states use that power to employ the statewide winner-take-all method. (Only Maine and Nebraska use a different allocation method, partly based on congressional districts.) That winner-take-all method is the root cause of so many people’s dislike of the Electoral College, because it awards all a state’s electors to one candidate, regardless of how close the popular vote margin is.

The most glaring example of this was Florida in 2000, when George W. Bush’s 537-vote popular vote win netted him all 25 of the state’s electoral votes and thus the presidency. The key to the compact is the understanding that whatever method a state chooses, it is only that — a choice — and one that a state’s legislature can change as it pleases.

There are legal obstacles too. In Michigan, voters in 2022 approved a series of amendments to the state Constitution, including, “The outcome of every election in this state shall be determined solely by the vote of electors casting ballots in the election.” That language may not have been targeting the compact but might appear to block it.

Mr. Koza told me he doesn’t agree, because the outcome of the Michigan election — that is, the total popular vote in the state — is still determined by Michigan voters. The choice of how to award Michigan’s electors is a separate process determined by the State Legislature.

Even if the compact survives in Michigan, there is no question it will face multiple legal challenges the moment it takes effect and could ultimately reach the Supreme Court. If a nonmember state were to sue the members of the compact, that case would go directly to the Supreme Court. In other words, this could all come to a head quickly.

The court would almost certainly weigh at least one straightforward constitutional question: Does the compact need the consent of Congress? The Constitution says consent is required for interstate compacts, but the Supreme Court has for more than a century interpreted that requirement to refer only to compacts that encroach on federal power.

As the court reiterated in 2020, the choice of how to award electors belongs exclusively to the states. The federal government has no role in the process. Consent of Congress should thus not be necessary, although with this Supreme Court, nothing should be taken for granted.

Finally there is that knotty partisan issue: If states led by Democratic governors have almost exclusively passed the compact, doesn’t it look like a plot to ensure that only Democrats win the White House? This framing has always mystified me. First, the most recent popular vote winner was a Republican. Second, the whole purpose of the compact is to benefit all voters in every corner of the country — Republicans no less than Democrats.

In addition, assumptions of broad Republican opposition to the popular vote may be oversold. From years of working with state lawmakers, Mr. Koza has found that many Republicans support the compact’s principles but have self-protective reasons for not saying so — starting with the man in the Oval Office. “If you’re voting against Trump, you’re attacking the way he was elected,” Mr. Koza told me, speaking of the 2016 election. “Frankly, it is fatal in a Republican primary. At least it has been.”

Pat Rosenstiel, a member of the compact team and a longtime Republican consultant, noted that polls showed increasing Republican support even before Mr. Trump’s win in 2024. After the 2016 election, only 27 percent of Republicans said they were on board with switching to popular election. A few weeks before the 2024 election, Pew found that number had jumped to 46 percent; it’s almost certainly higher today, after Mr. Trump won 2.3 million more votes than Kamala Harris.

Mr. Rosenstiel pointed out that there has been little resistance by those who oppose the compact in any of the 18 states that have joined it. The one exception is Colorado, where in 2020, opponents managed to get a referendum on the ballot in an attempt to reverse the state’s passing legislation the year before to join the compact. It didn’t work.

The future of the Electoral College may have been altered on election night this month for a second reason. Whenever people ask me what it would take to get more Republicans over the hump to support a popular vote for president, I say that it will happen when Texas turns blue. With 40 electoral votes, Texas is a bigger prize than any state but California, and it’s been solidly red for decades. This year, Democrats didn’t just do well in Texas; they dominated, winning every statewide race on the ballot.

If the Democratic candidate in 2028 were to win the most popular votes in Texas, suddenly a very plausible scenario, Republicans would lose all 40 of those electoral votes. The millions of Texans who vote for the Republican candidate would effectively disappear, just like the millions of Texas Democrats who have not cast a meaningful vote for president in nearly half a century.

Republicans are well aware of how much their electoral fortunes hinge on Texas. “Texas is the foundation of the Republican Party in America,” Don Huffines, the state’s comptroller, wrote on X late last month. “When the foundation breaks, it ALL falls apart.”

That is true — in an Electoral College world. Under a popular vote, those Texas Republicans’ votes would count just as much as everyone else’s all across America. I don’t know about you, but I find that a thrilling idea.

Right now, tens of millions of Americans’ ballots for president are effectively erased because they voted for the candidate who didn’t win in their state. And if you think you can predict how a popular vote election would turn out, don’t be so sure; battleground-state turnout data has long supported the claim that when people know their vote matters, more people vote.

Given all the evidence that the Electoral College today serves no one’s interests — except those of the swing states, several of which are now on the cusp of adopting the compact — I struggle to understand the remaining resistance to a national popular vote. The states’ interests are already well protected by their own governments, not to mention their two senators and their representatives in Washington.
The presidency is the only office whose occupant represents all Americans equally, wherever they live and whatever their politics. That’s the way anyone who wants the job should have to earn it, too.
